findings.title: PR record and target grammar are GitHub-flavored, undermining the "second host is a new implementation, not an edit" claim
findings.description:
The doc states "PR identity is a value, not a string" and fixes the typed record as `(host, owner, repository, number, base ref, head ref, head sha, URL)` — "every downstream consumer, including persistence and posting, keys on that record." It also says "A second host is a new implementation, not an edit" and that the protocol "must not leak `gh`-specific shapes so a direct-API or other-host implementation stays possible."

But the record's identity fields are GitHub-shaped: `owner`/`repository`/`number` is GitHub's `owner/repo#N` model. The Technical Considerations "Target grammar" section confirms this — the accepted shapes include `owner/repo#n`, which is GitHub's PR-fragment syntax. A GitLab merge request is `namespace/project!N` with potentially *nested* group namespaces, and uses a project-id or `!`-fragment identity rather than `#`. Forcing a second host into `owner`/`repository`/`number` either loses the nested-namespace structure or requires the protocol to carry host-specific identity alongside the "generic" fields — which is exactly the shape leakage the doc says it forbids. As written, the core record that "no component re-parses" is the thing a second host would have to bend around, so the "not an edit" claim is only true if the record is re-cut to be genuinely host-neutral (e.g., a host-opaque `repository_id` + host-supplied URL), which the doc does not propose. Slice design should either abstract the identity or stop asserting host-neutrality for the record.

findings.title: "The save path already accepts a generic save target in the CLI" overstates the persistence seam
findings.description:
The principle "Persistence takes a target, not a slice" asserts: "The save path already accepts a generic save target in the CLI; the PR review makes that generic on the persistence side too." Verified against `src/squadron/review/persistence.py` and `src/squadron/cli/commands/review.py`: the only genericity is the `target: SaveTargetT` type parameter threading through `_resolve_save_outcome`, which never reaches the persistence function. The actual save path is `SliceInfo`-hardwired end to end — `save_review_result(result, review_type, slice_info, ...)` builds the filename from `slice_info['index']` and `slice_info['slice_name']`, and `format_review_markdown` consumes `slice_info['slice_name']`/`['index']`/`['project']` (defaulting to `"unknown"`/`0` when `slice_info` is `None`). Every concrete caller passes a `SliceInfo`-shaped target and a `SliceInfo`-consuming `save` callable (`lambda info: _save_and_report(result, "code", info, ...)`).

So "a PR-keyed target satisfies the same contract" is not a small adaptation of an existing generic — there is no existing generic on the persistence side to attach to. Passing `slice_info=None` (the only way a PR review could reuse today's path) renders `slice: unknown`, `project: unknown`, index `0`, which collides with every other None-keyed review and satisfies neither the naming convention nor the frontmatter contract the doc requires. The PR-keyed-persistence slice is therefore a greenfield rework of the filename/frontmatter contract, and the doc's framing ("makes that generic on the persistence side too") understates it as an extension of something that exists rather than something that must be built. The doc also leans on 917's seams ("attaches to the seams 917 changes"), and slice 917 is `not_started` — so the "apply unchanged" claim rests on work that has not landed and whose shape could still move.

findings.title: Posting idempotency rests on an unspecified comment marker and an unresolved interaction with head movement
findings.description:
The Envisioned State says "A later invocation on the same PR updates or supersedes rather than stacking," and Technical Considerations says "The comment is marked so squadron can find and update its own prior comment." Two load-bearing details are unspecified:

1. **The marker mechanism.** The doc never says how the comment is "marked" so squadron can find its own prior comment among a PR's thread. This is the hard part of idempotency (a stable hidden marker, e.g. an HTML comment with a squadron key + head sha, that survives GitHub's comment rendering and that `gh` list-comments JSON still returns). Without it, "find and update its own prior comment" is asserted, not designed.

2. **The interaction with head movement.** "Base semantics" says a re-review against a PR whose head has moved "must say so," while "Posting idempotency" says update-or-supersede. These interact and the doc does not resolve them: on a second invocation where the reviewed head sha differs from the prior comment's, does squadron *update* the old (now stale) comment in place, *supersede* it by posting a new comment keyed to the new sha, or *refuse* until the operator confirms? Each has different correctness properties (an in-place update silently rewrites a review that was about a different commit; a supersede stacks unless the old is hidden). The "head sha recorded in the artifact is what was reviewed" invariant makes the choice load-bearing, and the doc leaves it open.

findings.title: `gh`-as-subprocess transport sits in an increasingly-async codebase, and the protocol is designed for reuse by a later pipeline path
findings.description:
The doc chooses `gh` as the transport and notes the cost is "a process boundary and JSON parsing per call." The existing precedent it would follow is `run_git` (`review/git_utils.py`), which is a blocking `subprocess.run` — fine for the sync CLI command bodies, where PR resolution and (later) posting would run around `asyncio.run(_execute_review(...))` exactly as `review_code` resolves its diff synchronously before the async call.

But the doc also says "A pipeline input for PR review is a later decision, taken only after the CLI has proven the shape," and "Interface parity… the `/sq:review` slash command and any later pipeline input accept identically." The pipeline review action (`pipeline/actions/review.py`) executes inside the executor's async context. A protocol whose operations are sync `subprocess.run` calls to `gh` — which the doc is defining now, as the contract the pipeline will later consume — would block the event loop when reused there, requiring `run_in_executor` wrapping at every call site or an async protocol surface. The doc frames `gh`-as-transport purely as an auth/enterprise-host convenience and does not address the sync/async fit of the protocol it is establishing for later reuse. The protocol shape chosen now (sync subprocess vs. awaitable) is load-bearing for the deferred pipeline work the doc explicitly anticipates, and the doc treats it as out of scope rather than as a design decision to make now.
